ch14_ex14_q1a: Degrees view: $\frac{\pi}{6}t$ radians is $30^\circ$ per hour, so 12 hours gives $360^\circ$, one full tide cycle.
Quarter-periods are 3 hours, so plot at $t = 0, 3, 6, \ldots, 24$; a 12-hour tidal cycle is close to real tides, a handy sense check.
ch14_ex14_q1b: High tide is a quarter-period after the rising zero at $t = 0$: $\frac{12}{4} = 3$; the next one is a full period later, $3 + 12 = 15$.
ch14_ex14_q1c: Because the centre line is mean sea level ($b = 0$), the high tide height is just the amplitude; the full range from high to low tide is $2 \times 5 = 10$ m.
ch14_ex14_q1d: At $30^\circ$ per hour, 2 a.m. is an angle of $60^\circ$, so the height is $5\sin 60^\circ$.
Sense check: 2 a.m. is one hour before high tide (3 a.m.), so the height should be close to, but below, 5 m.
ch14_ex14_q1e: 2 p.m. is $t = 14 = 2 + 12$, exactly one tidal period after 2 a.m., so you can copy that answer without new working.
ch14_ex14_q1f: 2.5 m is exactly half the amplitude, and $\sin u = \frac{1}{2}$ is a standard exact value: that is a hint the times will be whole hours.
The safe window is symmetric about high tide: $3 \pm 2$ gives 1 a.m. to 5 a.m.; add 12 hours for the afternoon window.
ch14_ex14_q2a: The greatest distance is centre plus amplitude, $3 + 2$; the $3$ inside $\sin(3t)$ only changes how fast it oscillates, not how far.
ch14_ex14_q2b: Since the centre (3) is bigger than the amplitude (2), the particle never reaches $O$, so it never changes side.
ch14_ex14_q2c: Maxima are one period apart: $\frac{2\pi}{3} \approx 2.09$ s. Starting from $\frac{\pi}{6} \approx 0.52$, keep adding $2.09$ until you pass 5.
ch14_ex14_q2d: $x = 3$ is the centre line, crossed every half-period ($\frac{\pi}{3} \approx 1.05$ s): $0, 1.05, 2.09$, and the next, $3.14$, is past 3.
ch14_ex14_q2e: Calculus link: velocity $\frac{dx}{dt} = 6\cos 3t$, so at $t = 0$ it moves at 6 m/s in the positive direction, the fastest it ever goes (passing through the centre).
ch14_ex14_q3a: With $\sin(2\pi t)$ the period is 1, so $t$ counts complete cycles directly; this is a common way to set up models with whole-number periods.
ch14_ex14_q3b: Centre minus amplitude: $5 - 2 = 3$; positive, so the particle stays on one side of $O$ and distance equals position.
ch14_ex14_q3c: First maximum is a quarter-period in: $\frac{1}{4}$ of 1 s, so $t = 0.25$; then add 1 s each time.
ch14_ex14_q3d: Each pair of solutions is symmetric about a maximum: $\frac{1}{12}$ and $\frac{5}{12}$ average to $\frac{3}{12} = 0.25$, the first maximum.
Then add the period (1 s) to each pair: $\frac{1}{12} + 1 = \frac{13}{12}$, $\frac{5}{12} + 1 = \frac{17}{12}$, and so on.
ch14_ex14_q3e: Calculus link: velocity is $4\pi\cos(2\pi t)$, so the particle starts at $x = 5$ moving at $4\pi \approx 12.6$ m/s in the positive direction.
ch14_ex14_q4ai: The centre of the circle is 10 m up and the radius is 10 m, so the lowest point of the circle just touches the ground.
ch14_ex14_q4aii: One revolution takes 6 s, so the particle turns $60^\circ$ each second; after 1 s it is $10\sin 60^\circ = 5\sqrt{3}$ m above the centre.
ch14_ex14_q4aiii: After 2 s the particle has turned $120^\circ$, and $\sin 120^\circ = \sin 60^\circ$: it is at the mirror-image point across the vertical diameter.
ch14_ex14_q4aiv: After 4 s it has turned $240^\circ$, so it is $5\sqrt{3} \approx 8.66$ m below the centre: $10 - 8.66 = 1.34$ m.
ch14_ex14_q4av: After 5 s it has turned $300^\circ$, the mirror image of $240^\circ$ across the vertical diameter, so the height matches $t = 4$.
ch14_ex14_q4b: Check with the circle: at $\frac{\pi}{3}$ radians per second, one full turn of $2\pi$ takes $2\pi \div \frac{\pi}{3} = 6$ s.
ch14_ex14_q4c: Greatest height = diameter = 20 m, since the lowest point is at ground level; it happens a quarter-period in, at $t = 1.5$ s.
ch14_ex14_q4d: 15 m is half a radius above the centre, so the particle has turned $30^\circ$ or $150^\circ$; at $60^\circ$ per second that is $0.5$ s and $2.5$ s.
ch14_ex14_q4e: Shortcut: 5 m is the reflection of 15 m in the centre line, and $\sin(u + \pi) = -\sin u$, so just add half a period (3 s) to the 15 m times: $0.5 + 3 = 3.5$, $2.5 + 3 = 5.5$.
ch14_ex14_q5a: With $-8\cos$, $t = 0$ gives the lowest value: centre minus amplitude, $17 - 8 = 9$.
ch14_ex14_q5b: Read the model directly: 17 is the average temperature and 8 is half the daily range, so the range is $17 \pm 8$.
Period is 24 h, so the maximum is half a period after the minimum at midnight: noon.
ch14_ex14_q5c: Solve only once: the graph is symmetric about the noon maximum, so if $T = 20$ at about 7:28 a.m. ($4$ h $32$ min before noon), it is also 20 at 4:32 p.m.
ch14_ex14_q5d: Since $-\cos u = \cos(u - \pi)$, the rule is also $T = 17 + 8\cos\left(\frac{\pi(t - 12)}{12}\right)$: an ordinary cosine with its peak shifted to noon.
The curve crosses the average 17 °C at 6 a.m. and 6 p.m., a quarter-period either side of noon.
ch14_ex14_q6a: Sketch the centre line $D = 10$ first, then dashed lines at $7$ and $13$; the curve touches each guide line once per 12-hour cycle.
ch14_ex14_q6b: 8.5 m is half the amplitude below the centre, so the low-water intervals are symmetric about each low tide: $9 \pm 2$ and $21 \pm 2$.
It is often easier to find when $D < 8.5$, namely $(7, 11)$ and $(19, 23)$, and take what is left of $[0, 24]$.
ch14_ex14_q6c: Why centre on the peak: moving the window either way lowers one of its ends, so the worst depth gets worse.
The window $[2.5, 3.5]$ has ends half an hour, i.e. $15^\circ$, from the peak at $90^\circ$; $\sin 75^\circ \approx 0.966$, giving $10 + 2.90 \approx 12.9$.
ch14_ex14_q7a: Cosine is the natural choice because $t$ is measured from high tide, where cosine already starts at its maximum; that is also why $q$ is positive.
High to low is half a period, so the period is 12 h and $r = \frac{360}{12} = 30$ degrees per hour.
ch14_ex14_q7b: At $30^\circ$ per hour, $t = 3$ gives $\cos 90^\circ = 0$, so the depth is at the centre value 5 m, confirming the quarter-period points.
ch14_ex14_q7c: 4 m is half the amplitude below the centre, so the times are symmetric about low tide ($t = 6$): the depth is below 4 m from $t = 4$ to $t = 8$.
Common slip: $t = 8$ is measured from high tide; subtract the 6 hours to low tide.
ch14_ex14_q8a: Check your model by its range: $4.5 \pm 1.5$ gives exactly $[3, 6]$. Any phase shift or a cosine version is also valid unless a starting condition is given.
ch14_ex14_q8b: Reality check: halfway between the extremes, near the equinoxes, the model gives 12 hours of daylight, matching day and night being about equal then.
Using cosine with $t = 0$ on the longest day means no phase shift is needed: start the clock at a maximum and cosine fits naturally.
